idiom_name: hub goroutine owning a subscriber map + per-subscriber channels (fan-out)
implementation_notes: Go replaces the classic registry object with its concurrency model: one long-lived goroutine owns the bus state (a map from event type or topic to a slice of subscriber channels) and a select loop over the inbound events, and publishers hand events in over a channel instead of calling a method on a shared registry ("do not communicate by sharing memory; instead, share memory by communicating"). Subscribe registers a fresh channel for the caller, publish fans the event out to every channel for that topic, and unsubscribe removes and closes the channel - no locks are needed because ownership of the map never leaves the hub goroutine. A synchronous registry of callbacks guarded by sync.RWMutex is still justified when delivery must be synchronous (tests, deterministic ordering) or when a goroutine per bus is unwanted; the standard library itself provides no broadcast bus.
pitfalls: A full subscriber channel silently loses events when the select falls through to default; a slow consumer should be detected and reported, not ignored.
An unbuffered subscriber channel blocks the hub and therefore every other subscriber, so the fan-out must never be a synchronous send on a channel the hub does not control.
Goroutine leaks: a subscriber that stops reading without unsubscribing keeps its channel and goroutine reachable, and the hub keeps sending; close channels from the hub side only.
Touching the subscriber map from any goroutine other than the owner reintroduces the data race the single-owner design was meant to remove.
